Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: Your friend calls you in the middle of the night, crying, because they just received some devastating family news.
Expectation2: Dress modestly according to Islamic guidelines.
Situation2: An office function with colleagues of all genders is scheduled this afternoon.
Story:
Last night, my phone buzzed at 2 a.m. It was Sara, her voice trembling as she told me her father had been rushed to the hospital. I sat up, heart pounding, listening to her sobs. She needed me, and I promised I’d be there for her, no matter what. I stayed on the line, offering words of comfort, feeling her pain as if it were my own. When the call ended, I barely slept, replaying her words and wondering how I could help her through this.

But as morning broke, another worry crept in. Today was the office function, a big event with colleagues from every department. The dress code was “business casual,” but I knew from past experience that my modest attire—long sleeves, loose pants, and a hijab—would stand out. Some colleagues had made comments before, and I dreaded the stares and questions. I wanted to support Sara, to be the friend she needed, but I also had to represent myself as a Muslim, upholding my values in a space where I already felt different. The weight of both roles pressed on me, and I felt torn, unsure how to be everything I was expected to be.
